questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: identify which federal court holds trials
questions.stem: A federal prosecutor files criminal charges against a person accused of bank robbery. Which federal court conducts the trial and imposes the sentence if the person is convicted?
questions.explanation: Article III created a single Supreme Court, and Congress built the rest of the federal system around district courts, which hold trials and impose sentences, with appeals running upward from them. The traps confuse an appellate court with a trial court or assume a federal crime belongs to the states, and either move the trial to a court that only reviews records or hand it to a system with no jurisdiction over the offence.
questions.hint: Which court hears witnesses first and returns the verdict?

provenance.author: bank-team-usg-b
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

options.text: The district court, because it is the federal system of trial courts
The court of appeals, because it reviews trials before sentencing
options.misconception: confuses the intermediate appellate court with a trial court

options.text: The Supreme Court, because it is the highest court in the country
options.misconception: believes the highest court is the one that hears witnesses

options.text: The state trial court, because robberies are state offences
options.misconception: assumes federal crimes are tried in the state courts

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
questions.learningObjective: identify the cases the Supreme Court hears first
questions.stem: Two states dispute where the border between them runs, and each files a case against the other. In which court does that case begin?
questions.explanation: The Constitution names a small set of cases the Supreme Court hears in the first instance, and suits between two states are among them, so the case starts there while every other matter reaches the Court only on appeal. The traps assume a universal rule of trial first, hand the dispute to a state court that cannot hear it against the other state, or promote an intermediate court to first-instance authority.
questions.hint: Which court hears a case between two states with no lower court first?

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

options.text: The Supreme Court, because suits between states begin there

options.misconception: treats a dispute between two states as an ordinary local suit

options.text: The court of appeals, because it reviews every federal dispute
options.misconception: gives an intermediate appellate court original authority

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Court of appeals as intermediate tier
questions.learningObjective: place a district court appeal in the court hierarchy
questions.stem: A district judge enters judgment in a federal civil case, and the losing side wants that ruling reviewed. Which court takes the appeal from the district court?
questions.explanation: Congress built three tiers: district courts try cases, courts of appeals review them, and the Supreme Court sits above both, so an appeal from a district court normally goes to a court of appeals rather than straight to the top. The alternatives skip the middle tier, treat review as a retrial by the same court, or route a federal appeal into a system with no role in it.
questions.hint: Which tier sits between the trial court and the top court?

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

options.misconception: believes a trial court reviews its own rulings after the fact

options.text: A state appellate court, because it hears all kinds of appeal
options.misconception: sends a federal appeal into the state court system

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Discretionary review and denial of review
questions.learningObjective: explain what a denial of review does and does not decide
questions.stem: A party asks the Supreme Court to take its case from a court of appeals, and the Court declines without giving reasons. What does that decision mean?
questions.explanation: The Court controls its docket through a written request to take a case, and a request it declines carries no view on the merits, so the earlier decision simply remains in force. Reading the refusal as a criticism, a reversal, or an endorsement invents a ruling where the process produced none, and each of those readings would treat the same refusal as decisive on a question the law left open.
questions.hint: Does declining to hear a case say anything about who was right?

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

options.text: The Court will not decide the case, and the lower ruling stands
The Court found the earlier ruling legally incorrect
options.misconception: reads a refusal to hear a case as a ruling against it

options.text: The Court has reversed the case and will now try it again
options.misconception: treats a declined request as a completed reversal

options.text: The Court has adopted the arguments of the losing party
options.misconception: assumes declining review signals agreement with the loser

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: identify the requirement for a case raising a federal issue
questions.stem: A homeowner sues a contractor in a state court, arguing that a federal statute sets the pricing rule for the contract. Both parties live in the same state. What must a federal court decide before taking the case?
questions.explanation: A federal court may take a case that arises under federal law, and a federal issue has to appear on the face of the complaint itself rather than emerge later in the litigation; the two parties here share a state, so no between-states rule is engaged. The traps turn a legal requirement into a preference, import a dollar floor from a different jurisdictional rule, or apply the rule that governs disputes between citizens of different states.
questions.hint: The issue has to be visible in the complaint itself. Which test?

options.text: Whether the two parties are citizens of different states

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: state the requirements for a federal case between citizens of different states
questions.stem: A plaintiff and a defendant who live in different states dispute a contract for ninety thousand dollars. Which set of requirements must hold before a federal court may hear the case?
questions.explanation: Where the parties are citizens of different states, a federal court may hear the dispute if the amount in controversy clears the statutory floor, and ninety thousand dollars does; this route does not require the claim to rest on federal law. The traps add a federal-issue requirement this route does not need, insist on citizenship by both rather than by one from each state, or swap the civil rule for the criminal one.
questions.hint: Which two conditions does this route to federal court impose?

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: apply the quorum rule to a nine-seat court
questions.stem: The nation's highest court has nine members. How many must be present for the Court to hear argument and announce a decision on a case?
questions.explanation: Eight of the nine seats must be filled for the Court to sit, so a single vacancy leaves a quorum of eight while a second vacancy leaves the Court unable to decide anything, and the votes needed to grant review are a separate count from the votes needed to decide. Taking a majority of nine, requiring all nine, or counting the votes to grant review each substitutes a different number for the one the rule supplies.
questions.hint: Nine seats, and one vacancy does not stop the Court. How many is that?

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: apply a statutory panel requirement to a challenge of a state law
questions.stem: A federal statute requires a district court to hear a certain kind of challenge to a state law with a panel rather than a single judge. How many judges must sit on that panel?
questions.explanation: For a narrow class of challenges to state action the statute specifies a three-judge district panel, so three is fixed by the text rather than derived from a general rule, and the ordinary practice of one judge per district case does not apply. Substituting the default, an even number chosen to prevent ties, or the size of the top bench each supplies a familiar number that the statute never uses.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: apply the unanimity rule to a twelve-person criminal jury
questions.stem: A person stands trial for a serious federal crime before a jury of twelve. How many members must agree before the court may record a guilty verdict?
questions.explanation: A federal criminal jury has twelve members and a guilty verdict must be unanimous, so the count is all twelve rather than a bare majority or a supermajority short of unanimity, and the quorum rule from another court in the same system has nothing to do with it. Each trap number comes from a rule that does not govern criminal verdicts, and a court applying any of them would convict without the agreement the guarantee requires.
questions.hint: There is no supermajority short of unanimity in a federal trial.

options.misconception: borrows the quorum rule from the highest court bench

options.text: Ten members, because ten of twelve is a strong majority

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: compute a share of dispositions against the full docket
questions.stem: A district court report lists how its cases ended this year: three hundred sixty by settlement, two hundred seventy by dismissal, one hundred eighty by summary judgment, and ninety by trial. About what share of all cases ended by settlement?
questions.explanation: The four categories add to 900 cases and settlements account for 360 of them, so 360 divided by 900 is 0.40, or two of every five cases. Each other figure is arithmetically sound but describes a different disposition, and the choice between them comes down to using the whole docket as the base rather than one category or a convenient subset of two.
questions.hint: Add the four categories before dividing anything.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: apply the standing requirements to a prospective plaintiff
questions.stem: A law takes effect next month, and a person who will be affected by it wants to sue today. Before a federal court will hear the dispute, what must that person show?
questions.explanation: A federal court needs a case or controversy, which requires an actual injury traceable to the party bringing the suit that a favorable ruling could remedy, and generalized complaints about how government works do not qualify. The traps let anyone sue on a theory, demand uniqueness rather than concreteness, or convert a public grievance into a private injury, none of which is what the requirement asks for.
questions.hint: Concreteness, traceability, and a remedy that helps this person.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: decide whether a claim about a future law is ripe
questions.stem: A legislature has passed a law but has set its start date for next year, and a group of people who expect to be affected file suit today. How should a court treat the case?
questions.explanation: Ripeness keeps courts from deciding disputes that have not yet hurt anyone, and a law that has not taken effect produces no present injury, so a claim about how it will operate waits until it applies to someone. The traps substitute milestones that are not harm, such as fixed text, a filing, or a calendar date, and each would let a court resolve a controversy that does not yet exist.
questions.hint: Timing matters here: has the law touched anyone yet?

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: decide whether a dispute remains live after the facts change
questions.stem: A person sued over a licence scheduled to expire next year, and the licensing authority has now cancelled the licence before the trial date. What happens to the case?
questions.explanation: Mootness asks whether the dispute is still alive, and a licence that no longer exists removes the controversy the plaintiff needed, leaving the court nothing to decide, though the answer would differ if the same harm were likely to recur and could not be reviewed in time. The traps treat a past injury as permanently live, freeze the facts at filing, or borrow a ground that asks who may sue rather than what is left to sue about.
questions.hint: Ask what is still in dispute, not what was once true.

questions.topic: Civil jury right and its threshold
questions.learningObjective: apply the civil jury guarantee to a stated amount in controversy
questions.stem: A person sues a neighbour in federal court for damages and never asks for a jury. In a civil claim of forty-five thousand dollars, what does the constitutional guarantee provide?
questions.explanation: The civil jury guarantee reaches suits at common law where the amount in controversy exceeds the stated floor, and forty-five thousand dollars clears it comfortably, while what the guarantee supplies is a right to request the jury that a party gives up by not asking in time. Reading it as automatic, as criminal-only, or as requiring the other side consent each removes the choice the guarantee leaves to the party.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: apply the bar on duplicate prosecution to two separate governments
questions.stem: After a robbery, a person is charged by the state and then separately by federal agents for the same act. What does the constitutional bar on duplicate prosecution do here?
questions.explanation: The bar on duplicate prosecution restrains a sovereign from retrying the same person for the same offence, and that restraint runs between separate sovereigns, so a state prosecution and a federal prosecution of the same act may both proceed. The traps either extend the bar across sovereigns, which the rule does not do, or substitute a hierarchy of laws and a cost argument for a question about who holds the power to prosecute.
questions.hint: Ask which authority is bringing the second prosecution.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: distinguish testimonial and physical evidence under the self-incrimination rule
questions.stem: Investigators tell a suspect that he may leave unless he answers questions about the robbery. Which part of that exchange does the protection against compelled self-incrimination cover?
questions.explanation: The protection against compelled self-incrimination reaches compelled testimonial communication, so answers extracted by pressure cannot be used against the speaker, but it does not reach fingerprints or a blood sample because that evidence exists independently of any statement. Extending it to physical evidence, or narrowing it to writing, misreads the line the rule draws around compelled speech rather than around the person.
questions.hint: The rule protects what a person says, not what a person is.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: identify the process due before a government takes a property interest
questions.stem: A city collects a small payment from a shop owner under a rule adopted long ago, and gives the owner neither a hearing nor a chance to object. Which guarantee is at issue?
questions.explanation: When a government takes a property interest through an administrative process, the guarantee of due process requires notice of the charge and a real opportunity to respond before the taking becomes final, so a hearing skipped at the outset makes the process defective even where the amount is small. Confusing this with substantive due process, equal protection, or a power clause points at a different subject: the fairness of the result, the treatment of comparable groups, or the reach of a power.

questions.topic: Applying national guarantees to the states
questions.learningObjective: explain what is required before a national guarantee binds a state

questions.explanation: The Bill of Rights restrains the national government directly, so extending one of its guarantees to a state requires a judicial ruling that the Fourteenth Amendment carries it there, and the reasoning for that ruling matters as much as the result. questions.stem: A new law is challenged in federal court, and the challengers offer no evidence about the facts the legislature relied on. How does a court ordinarily treat a law that has been duly enacted?
questions.explanation: Courts begin from the proposition that a duly enacted law is valid, so the party challenging it must show that no set of facts the legislature could reasonably have found makes the law workable, and the absence of published reasons is not itself a defect. questions.explanation: A classification drawn along a line the law treats as inherently suspect is judged against the demanding standard, which asks the government to show a compelling need and to draw the line as narrowly as the need allows, and the party challenging it does not get the ordinary presumption of validity. questions.topic: Guarantees not yet applied to the states
questions.learningObjective: count the guarantees that do not yet bind the states
questions.stem: A state is asked to apply the whole Bill of Rights to its own courts and officials. Which description matches what that change would produce?
questions.explanation: Applying the whole Bill of Rights to the states would add the two guarantees courts have not held to restrict state and local government, the bar on compelling quartering of soldiers in homes and the bar on cruel and unusual punishment, while every other guarantee already reaches the states. Statements about first-time protection everywhere, about no change at all, or about a withdrawal each contradict the way the guarantees are presently divided between the two levels.
questions.hint: Count the guarantees that no ruling has yet applied to a state.

provenance.author: bank-team-usg-b
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

options.text: Two guarantees would bind the states for the first time
Every guarantee would bind the states for the first time
options.misconception: believes no guarantee has yet been applied to the states

options.text: No guarantee would change, since all already bind the states
options.misconception: assumes the Bill of Rights already reaches every level

options.text: One guarantee would be withdrawn from the states
options.misconception: thinks application to states removes a right from them

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Counsel for those who cannot afford it
questions.learningObjective: describe the current reach of the right to appointed counsel
questions.stem: A court once provided a lawyer to an indigent defendant only when the government sought the death penalty, and the rule has since been widened. Which description matches the widening?
questions.explanation: The guarantee of counsel to those who cannot afford one now reaches every felony prosecution and every case in which a person can actually be locked up, a clear extension of an earlier rule confined to death-penalty cases. Each other description draws the line where the current rule does not, at serious offences short of a felony, at capital cases, or at no threshold at all, and each would leave some people facing prison without counsel.
questions.hint: What reaches a person who will actually be locked up?

provenance.author: bank-team-usg-b
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

options.text: Every felony prosecution, and any case with real imprisonment
Only serious offences, leaving misdemeanours to the defendant
options.misconception: keeps the older rule for every case short of a felony

options.text: Only capital cases, since a life sentence is not serious
options.misconception: thinks the widening stops short of life sentences

options.text: Every criminal case, whatever penalty the law allows
options.misconception: extends the rule to cases with no imprisonment at all

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Regulatory taking of all viable use
questions.learningObjective: identify when a regulation requires compensation
questions.stem: A regulation leaves an owner with no reasonable use of the remaining land, though the owner keeps legal title and physical possession. What must the government do?
questions.explanation: A regulation that takes all economically viable use of property works a taking of that property even though the government holds no title and the owner keeps possession, and compensation is then owed because the test looks at practical loss of use rather than at the paper record. A licence, a repeal, or silence each leave the owner without the payment the guarantee requires.
questions.hint: The test asks about practical loss of use, not about who holds paper.

provenance.author: bank-team-usg-b
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

options.text: Pay just compensation for the property that was taken
Offer a licence so the owner may keep the same use
options.misconception: thinks a licence cures a denial of all use

options.text: Return the title and abandon the regulation entirely
options.misconception: confuses compensation with repeal of the regulation

options.text: Do nothing, because regulation alone never requires payment
options.misconception: believes any regulation escapes the compensation duty

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: explain why the same guarantee binds one level of government and not the other
questions.stem: Explain why the same conduct can be lawful for a federal officer and unlawful for a state officer, and name the step that produces the difference.
questions.explanation: A strong answer names the direct restraint on the national government, identifies the Fourteenth Amendment as the route by which the same guarantee reaches state officers, and explains that the ruling on that route is what changes the result. Answers resting on policy preference, or on the belief that the Bill of Rights always reached both levels, never reach the legal step.
questions.hint: Name the route, then name what travels along it.

provenance.author: bank-team-usg-b
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

answer.exemplar: The Bill of Rights restrains the national government on its own, so a federal officer is bound directly by the guarantee it contains, while a state officer is bound only once a court has held that the Fourteenth Amendment applies that same guarantee to the states. That holding is the step that produces the difference, and it has to rest on the content of the guarantee itself rather than on policy preference. An answer that says one level obeys the Constitution and the other obeys the states, or that assumes the Bill of Rights always covered both levels, stops before the step that does the work.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Two grounds for refusing to decide
questions.learningObjective: distinguish two grounds for declining a case and their separate cures
questions.stem: A court dismisses one case because the harm the plaintiff suffered has already been repaired, and dismisses another because the plaintiff is not the right person to bring it. Explain how those two reasons differ and what would become of each claim if the underlying dispute were still unresolved.
questions.explanation: A strong answer treats one ground as a question about whether anything is left to decide and the other as a question about who may decide it, then explains that only the second is fixed by choosing a better party while the first requires a live dispute. Answers that treat the grounds as interchangeable, or that say one of them can never be cured, misstate what each one depends on.
questions.hint: Separate the question of what is left from the question of who may ask.

provenance.author: bank-team-usg-b
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

answer.exemplar: The first ground asks whether the case is still worth deciding, because the controversy the plaintiff needed has been repaired, while the second asks who is permitted to decide it, because the person filing is not the one with the injury. A restored dispute cures the first only when the person who sues is also the proper party, and a proper plaintiff cannot revive a dispute that has ended, since nothing is left for the court to resolve. Answers that treat the grounds as interchangeable, or that describe one of them as permanent, miss that each has its own cure and its own limit.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Which reading of a state rule governs
questions.learningObjective: evaluate which construction of a state rule a federal court must follow
questions.stem: An original study of a contract dispute describes a federal court hearing a case between parties from two different states. The judge reads a state contract clause in a way the research of the study suggests is doubtful, and the study notes the state high court has already read that clause differently. What should the study conclude about the reading?
questions.explanation: A federal court hearing a dispute between citizens of different states applies the law of the state in which it sits, including the reading given by that state high court, so the state reading controls and the federal court own contrary reading is not a sound basis for the result it announced. Treating the federal reading as decisive, splitting the question between systems, or preferring the view of the study each denies where the authority to interpret that rule actually sits.
questions.hint: Ask which court has the last word on a question of its own law.

provenance.author: bank-team-usg-b
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

options.text: The reading given by the state high court is the one that governs
The federal reading governs, because that court heard the case first
options.misconception: assumes the first court to hear a case settles a state question

options.text: Both readings apply, one in each of the two court systems
options.misconception: splits a single question of state law between the systems

options.text: The study should pick whichever reading it finds better
options.misconception: substitutes scholarly preference for the governing legal source
